name: Jaw exerciser

lead: A jaw exerciser is a silicone or plastic ball, bar or resistance trainer that you bite or chew against to work the masseter and other chewing muscles. It is promoted on social media for a sharper jawline and a reduced double chin.

The masseter attaches at the angle of the jaw and can enlarge in people who clench, grind or chew gum constantly, so the idea is that a bigger masseter changes the lower face. That growth widens the jaw angle rather than removing chin fat. A 2024 case report of two people using a commercial device for about three months found no noticeable change in jaw appearance.

paras: Users chew or bite against the device in short sessions, often daily, alongside hard gum and chewing routines. Muscle changes would take weeks to months.

Overuse can strain the temporomandibular joint and cause jaw pain, headaches and tooth wear. People with TMJ symptoms are generally advised to avoid them. The chewing muscles do not directly affect chin fat or skin tightness.

angle.text: Users chew against silicone devices to build the masseter for a sharper jawline and less double chin. Chewing can grow the muscle, which widens the lower face; a 2024 case report of two users found no noticeable change in jaw appearance.

lead: A jaw exerciser is a handheld or mouth-worn resistance device, usually made of silicone or plastic and often shaped like a ball, bar or pair of plates, that the user bites or chews against to train the muscles of mastication, chiefly the masseter. Products in this category are sold under names such as Jawzrsize and are promoted on social media for a more defined jawline and reduced double chin. [1][2][3] The same term and similar devices also exist in clinical practice, where jaw exercisers are used in rehabilitation of restricted mouth opening. [4][5][6]

The masseter is a thick muscle that raises the lower jaw and attaches at the angle of the mandible. Wikipedia reports that the muscle can enlarge in people who habitually clench or grind their teeth and in those who constantly chew gum, and that this enlargement is generally soft and painless. [7] The idea behind cosmetic jaw exercisers is that a larger masseter will change the appearance of the lower face. [3][1]

A 2024 case report of two people who used a commercial jaw exerciser for about three months found no noticeable changes in jaw appearance, and its authors reported that a review of the literature found limited evidence that these devices reduce double chins, enhance jawlines or tighten facial skin, noting that the mastication muscles do not directly affect submental fat or skin elasticity. [3] No controlled trial of cosmetic jaw exercisers on jawline definition was found. Studies on masticatory muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics after chewing exist, but they concern gum chewing, not these devices. [8][9]

paras: Cosmetic jaw exercisers are used by biting, squeezing or chewing against a firm resistance for sets of repetitions. Some are balls placed between the teeth, some are bars or two-plate devices, and others are mouthpieces moulded around the teeth. Patent filings for jaw exercisers describe devices of widely different purposes, including a 1991 jaw exerciser applying controlled force for facial orthopedics, a 1999 custom-fit strengthener moulded over the teeth, and a 2007 device with opposing plates and a handle to alleviate temporomandibular joint pain. [10][11][12]

In oral and maxillofacial surgery, jaw exercisers have been used for decades after procedures for temporomandibular joint ankylosis and similar conditions to maintain mouth opening. A 1975 paper described a new jaw exerciser for postoperative use in ankylosis, case reports from 1985 and 1986 described a jaw exerciser for fibrous ankylosis, and a case report on oral submucous fibrosis described mouth-opening exercises with a jaw exerciser for six months after surgery, with mouth opening maintained at 32 mm at 18 months. [4][5][6][13] These clinical uses are rehabilitative and are not studies of cosmetic effect.

The masseter has superficial, deep and coronoid heads and inserts into the angle and ramus of the mandible; it is innervated by the trigeminal nerve and is one of the strongest muscles of mastication. [7] Wikipedia notes that masseteric hypertrophy can occur with bruxism or constant gum chewing and may produce a squarer lower face, and sometimes asymmetry when enlargement is unequal. [7]

Proponents argue that resistance training of the masseter increases its size and definition. The authors of the 2024 case report observe that the muscles worked are not those that determine submental fat or skin tension, and conclude that cosmetic claims about double chin or skin tightening are not well supported. [3] Grokipedia's article on the masseter likewise describes its anatomy and the effects of hypertrophy, although it is an AI-generated source. [1]

Evidence on cosmetic use is limited to a single report. In a 2024 case report in Cureus, two people used a commercially available jaw exerciser for about three months following the product's instructions; neither reported noticeable changes in jaw appearance by subjective measurement, and the authors reviewed the broader literature and found the overall evidence inconclusive. [3][14]

Related studies concern gum chewing rather than jaw exercisers. A 2021 study used shear wave elastography to monitor changes in masticatory muscle stiffness after gum chewing, and a 2024 study examined the effect of gum chewing training on masseter muscle oxygen dynamics. [8][9] Clinical reports of jaw exercisers in ankylosis and mouth-opening rehabilitation exist but do not address cosmetic outcomes. [4][6][13][15]

Wikipedia notes that masseter enlargement can be mistaken for conditions such as salivary gland disease or dental infection, and that habitual clenching and grinding are associated with hypertrophy. [7] The wiki's site note raises the possibility that overuse of chewing devices might aggravate the temporomandibular joint; no published trial has measured the rate of such effects from cosmetic jaw exercisers. Bruxism and temporomandibular disorders are discussed in the related entry on night guards.

Jaw exercisers are discussed in looksmax.org threads asking which device is best and whether buying exercisers on Amazon will produce masseter hypertrophy. [16][17] A T Nation post from 2013 told a poster to look up Jawzrsize, treating it as a joke solution to a different problem, which illustrates the product's name recognition outside looksmaxxing. [2]
